Shouzhi was named Qianyi, a man of Changshu, and served as Grand Master of Rites. Tianchi was named Ne, a man of Changshu. Assistant Censor Jin was named Xuezeng, sobriquet Xingwu. Ministry Official Yu was named Chunxi, sobriquet Deyuan, both men of Qiantang. Deyuan wrote the preface to the Eastern Journey Collection.)

Fuzheng observes: in this year, the first half of the chronicle gives the origin of the Fayun Temple on Wuru Peak. The latter half gives the origin of the Eastern Journey Collection: at Jinsha, Qu’a, Wumen, and Wulin, the faithful and Dharma companions of that time, among whom Fuzheng came to take refuge in the Master, was given the name Fuzheng and the courtesy name Liangsheng. In the whole chronicle the great junctures are: first the reverence paid to the First Patriarch, next to the Sixth Patriarch, and now to the Fourth and Fifth Patriarchs — each one following the season’s occasion, face to face seal and attestation, the flesh-body heir of the Patriarchs: marvellous and great indeed. When the Master reached the Jizhao Hut at Shuangjing, Fuzheng was lodging at West Lake in the Liaozhai, reading. Because of the collapse of the great building and the shelter of three beams, and the karmic cause of his rebirth, he hurried to Mount Jing to pay his respects to Chan Master Xueqiao, and in the Qianzhi Hut that had been built before, he was urged to lead in person the worship of the Liang Emperor’s Repentance; when the seven days were done he at once gained ease and lightness of body and mind. He vowed to press on with vigour and did not return home from the mountain, and it happened that at the Jizhao Hut he met the Master, who had come up the mountain to cremate Master Daguan — the very day on which the Master opened the sacrificial text sealed at Nanyue, without a day’s discrepancy. Yan Shengsheng was a man of Tongxiang county living at Shimen, Fuzheng’s fellow graduate, and the father of Kaimei, whose name was Junyan. One evening he had beforehand dreamed of the temple guardian spirit, who bade him welcome Piṇḍola; he saw one seated in the central hall in the place of honour, with attendants seated to either side, all famous elders of the time, masters of Dharma and Vinaya, those he had known in the past — all were there, and he woke with a start. The next day he heard that the Master was coming east, and he ordered a boat to go and welcome him at Songling, and travelled with him through Shuangjing, Yunqi, and the hills about the lake. Wherever they went, he attended the Master longest along with Fuzheng, and was named Fujian. Later, when the Master returned and passed through Shimen, Shengsheng invited him to his home, where there was a troupe of players; the Master ordered them to perform The Pavilion of Moon-Worship, and a great offering was made. Only those attendants who had received full ordination were first chosen and permitted to sit at the feast; all the rest were forbidden. Among those seated at the time were such famous elders as Chaosong, Yiyu, Zhihe, Wengu, Gude, Foshi, Dezong, Xinzong, Xuanjin, and others. In the course of the feast Shengsheng said to Fuzheng: “This is clear and distinct — the very scene of people and setting I saw in my dream of Piṇḍola.” The next day Fuzheng, in the Dharma boat, asked: “Does watching a play hinder the precepts?” The Master sighed and said: “Very hard to say. Another man who does not break the precepts for a day is for that day not breaking the precepts. I who do not break the precepts day after day am day after day breaking the precepts.” Hearing this, Fuzheng felt his heart sink and his courage fail, and to this day the words are still in his ears. The Essentials of Chan Practice and the Song of the Pole-Carrier were both preached for the assembly in the great hall of Mount Jing. It is widely said in various quarters that the Song of the Pole-Carrier was written for Chan Master Xueqiao, but this is a great error. Master Xue stood alone, lofty and steep, and was out of tune with many famous Chan masters; only with our Master was he in unbroken accord. The Master wrote for him the True Praise of the Mountain Master Xueqiao and the Six Wonders Inscription of the Qianzhi Hut. As he was about to leave, he again received from Master Xue the offering of an iron ruyi and wrote an inscription for it; all of this is in the Eastern Journey Collection, and reading it one may know the occasion of their meeting and accord. Therefore I record the Song of the Pole-Carrier here, to resolve the doubts that arise in the Dharma gate.

Song of the Pole-Carrier, with preface: The Dharma cavern of Mount Jing, since Dahui revived the way of Linji, has continued the wisdom-life without a break, and each generation has had its men. Of late the Chan gate has been desolate and its echoes have long ceased. Just now there gathered in the mountain a whole company of students investigating Chan, some of whom, at a single thought, glimpsed the ground and had it appear before them, attaining great freedom. It is a pity that, seated on that pure white ground, they are unwilling to let it go, thinking it extraordinary, not knowing that it becomes a hindrance to the Dharma; in the teachings it is called the obstruction of the knowable. Therefore the ancient worthy said: Even if you can reach the point of a cold pool and bright moon, of the bell-sound in the still night, unimpaired by any knock, undispersed by any wave, it is still a matter on the shore of birth and death. It is as said: In a thicket of thorns it is easy to set foot, but beneath the bright moon’s curtain it is hard to turn the body. This is called clutching the tip of the pole, sitting still in dead water. Even that is not permitted to be dwelt in, much less the case of one who has not yet reached the glimpse of the ground, who has by chance obtained a lightning-flash samadhi and thinks he has attained it, juggling the shadows of the conscious spirit. This is the common ailment of all ages: to be satisfied with a little in Chan. I feared it would fall into the world’s way and spread, misleading many. When someone asked for instruction, I smiled and showed him the Song of the Pole-Carrier. The song says: Pole-carrier, pole-carrier, why so sorely cheated? You want your shoulder light, your stumbling heel unheeded. Though you should bear it back before your birth began, it has long since hidden half of you from man. This board, this cangue upon your neck is hung, and all your flesh and bone to it are bound; if you do not cast it off while it is new, through a hundred thousand kalpas it will prove your foe at last. Sitting, it wearies you; walking, it wearies too. It is plainly a hindrance — why can you not see? Only because at first you took the false for true, a demon breeds within a house of purity. Eyes open, you see it; eyes shut, you see it still; by day the void sprouts lightning in the skies. The Gandharva city rises as a shadow in the air, and the foolish child takes it for paradise. Would you be light? Then you must put it down. What price is a stinking dead toad worth, I pray? Black beans traded in for your own eyes — you must discern the fish-eye from the true alway. There is a road, and it is the best to tread, broad and level as a balance-beam: only do not dally by the flowers and willows, and you shall surely reach the imperial city, I deem. Cast off body and life as if the great earth, nor shun to be ox or horse, camel or ass. If you can truly toss them beyond Sumeru, the sword-tree and the knife-hill are but child’s play. Love it, and by it you shall be undone; its burdens come of all the care you spend. One morning when the crystal flask is broken, the earth and all its hills are shattered to the end. I counsel you: do not carry it at all. The sweat upon a skull dries straight away. Divide your body, scatter your shadow into millions; from now you shall not enter death’s gate, come what may.

Fuzheng further notes: what the Master’s own chronicle records of himself sets down only the outline and has no leisure to set down the details. The commentary that Fuzheng has written likewise obtains only one tenth of what he saw and heard, and omits nine tenths. For instance, in this year’s entry, “he was willing to be the patron for the building at Mount Kuang,” and in the next year’s entry, “Lord Wang, who had already provided the funds to build the quiet hut” — such a faithful patron and official is called only “Minister of War Wang,” with no full name and no native place. Reading it in the past, I supposed it must be the former Minister of War Wang Boyu; but the years are far apart and Chu and She are distant from each other, which was just what I could not explain. Lately, seeing the Master’s Dharma kinsman Master Rongcheng, I learned that it was Lord Jingfeng, who lived at Huangmei and served as supreme commander. So then the omissions among the faithful who took refuge in him are past counting. Again, in that year’s entry, when he reached Jinzhu Ping at Mount Kuang, there are the four words “viewed all its beauties,” which must embrace I know not how many events of the bodhimanda. For example, at Jiujiang there is the bodhimanda of Master Yuan of Shimen, where the Master dwelt for a month and preached, and the man he appointed as abbot there was Master Rongcheng. He had first been a student of Xiuning, of the surname Cheng and the name Keyu; he studied at Shimen with the layman Bi Guanzhi, and at his first sight of the Master he abandoned his home, took refuge, and was shaved, receiving the Dharma name Guangshel, and was then appointed abbot of the Shimen bodhimanda. Later, when the Master was at Wuru, he repeatedly sent handwritten letters charging him to manage the affairs of Shimen, and his instructions were earnest and pressing; this was his closest Dharma heir at the time, yet the chronicle has no leisure to record it. One day Master Rong, with Shao Shisheng, brought various writings in the Master’s own hand to the Ou-xie Dwelling at the Rain-Flower Terrace, burned incense, recited them, and so wrote a note to record it. Another day the master Shaoxuan, whose Dharma name was Ciyi, came from Jiangyin to visit; he was the Dharma grandson of Master Zhiwei and the Dharma heir of Master Cimen. He had once lived at Fayun, later at the One-Bowl Chan Grove in Xunyang, and had also restored the Xiujing Temple at Hongshan in Wuchang. In the chaos of war he buried bones wherever he went and twice established land-and-water rites. He was by birth a son of the Lu family of Jiangyin; after the dynastic change he returned to his village and is now restoring the Wanfo Chan Grove. He says that the disciples he has saved, such as Renda and Liangming, are very many, but that he never had the chance to attend the Master in person. Of the chief disciples whom the Master most approved, none equalled Master Zhiwei, whose name was Fushan. In the beginning he shared good and ill fortune with the Master, appearing six times in the chronicle of the Master’s approaching death; in the end he ran about supporting the reliquary and recorded in detail the karmic circumstances of the Master’s last affairs. He is the true son of Wuru. Again there is Master Xuzhong, whose name was Guangyi: at the Baolin assembly he personally witnessed the nirvana, begged the Master to let down his foot, and transmitted his dying words — all clearly attested; he is the adopted grandson of Caoxi. Now Master Zhiwei’s great-great-grandson Renxi, styled Mingji, studies the Dharma at Changgan; and Master Xuzhong has a disciple Ciren, styled Jianru, who is abbot of Qixia. It was these too whom Fuzheng, after the chaos, met by karmic chance while lodging in the old capital of Nanking, and who brought the chronicle and commentary to completion. Among these, the circumstances of the Master’s last affairs, as heard from Kuanju, whose name was Guangyong, are especially detailed and accurate. The many later accounts are all untrustworthy, and I dare not set them down rashly. I regret that he passed away so suddenly at Qixia, and did not live to see the chronicle and commentary completed. Kuanju was in truth the heir of Zhiwei and the grandfather of Mingji. Again, at one time, going back and forth to the Patriarch’s Hall and the Bao’en Temple, there was one whom Fuzheng met when Master Su of Lingfeng was preaching: Master Huaibai, whose name was Hengdao, who had lived at Fayun for more than two years, attended the Master closely, and received the full precepts from him. And the prior of the Patriarch’s Hall, Zhanchi, whose name was Xiuru, was the grandson of Great Master Xuelang and the direct heir of the revered elder brother whom the Master often remembered. All these gentlemen, together with Master Su of Lingfeng, had deep Dharma bonds, and by rule are recorded here after the Dharma lineage.

From taking refuge in that year onward, in all matters of attending closely on the Master, Fuzheng began to call him “our Master.” At first he enshrined and honoured his Dharma image at the Dragon-Tree Altar of Mount Yao, and later at the Ou-xie Dwelling of the Rain-Flower Terrace — this when the monk Juelang was preaching in the Three Treasures Hall, and he specially led the assembled attendants to do reverence at the feet of the one who presided there. Now that Master Su is again preaching in the Three Treasures Hall, Fuzheng has been able to take counsel with him and bring the excellent work of the chronicle and commentary to completion; the whole origin of it is recorded here.

Master Su was of the Zhong family; in his youth he lived at Sumen and studied the Confucian classics, firmly believing in Confucius, whom he often saw in dreams. At seventeen, reading Master Lian’s writings, he first awakened to the Pure Land. At twenty-two, through Master Xueling Jun’s Key to the Contemplation Hymn he came into accord with our Master, went to Mount Kuang to consult him, and there, offering a stick of incense, asked about the Dharma. The Master showed the layman Zhong a verse: “The West lies only in your own heart’s head; when afflictions are empty, deluded thoughts are stilled. Then you will see Amitābha’s true face: he comes of old, from the sea of suffering, sailing his boat of compassion.” Two years later he relied on Master Xue, abandoned his home, and was shaved. From then until the Master’s passing into cessation there were four occasions of dream-karma. Now he expounds the Tiantai school and points the way to the Pure Land — the Dharma milk that Fuzheng witnessed with his own eyes.
The Forty-Fifth Year, Dingyi ●

I was seventy-two. On the first day of the first month of spring I expounded the precepts for the assembly. I went down from Shuangjing to mourn at Yunqi; more than a thousand black-robed and white-robed disciples had long been waiting in the mountain, and I stayed twenty days. Every night I gave informal instruction and answered questions on the Dharma; each was filled with joy, and I set forth the secret practices of Master Lianchi’s life. Some disciples wept to hear it, saying that I had revealed what others did not know, and they asked me to write his stupa inscription. When I left the mountain, Master Xuanjin and the scholar Tan Mengxun, with the gentry and laymen of the prefecture, invited me to stay at the Zongjing Hall of Jingci; for days thousands of fingers were raised around me as I expounded the great precepts, and I wrote the Record of the Zongjing Hall. At that time all the famous worthies of every quarter gathered about the lake, and with the scholar Tan asked about the Dharma, each pressing his own hard questions; it was called the greatest Dharma assembly of the southeast, such as had never been seen before. Then I visited Lingyin, the Three Zhu, and the Western Hills, and praised the three ponds of releasing life, and so departed. At that time the officials and laymen of the city provided boats to release living creatures and gave me a farewell feast on the lake, and moreover drew up a petition asking me to stay at Yunqi; so there was a promise of three years. Passing Zhili, the vice-minister Yue Shifan and the assistant prefect Xiang Chudong, old acquaintances of mine, met me at the Lengyan Chan Cloister. It happened that Shen Lübo of Linxi welcomed me to his home, and in the midst of the gathering he suddenly asked where the stupa of the former Master Yungu was, saying he did not know its whereabouts. The layman told him at once: “Near, quite near — about a li from Qizhen.” I was overjoyed, and that evening I went to the temple and did reverence at my late master’s stupa. I saw that the temple was most secluded and lovely, while the stupa court was rather desolate; I was sad for a long while. Regretting that my journey was hurried and I could not set it in order, I respectfully asked Mr. Shen to repair it in my stead, and charged him to establish a long-life field to support the incense and lamps. Of all that I passed by on that journey, the writings I made at the time were collected by Master Xuanjin He and the scholar Tan Mengxun into four fascicles and printed under the title Eastern Journey Collection. Returning to Wumen, the two masters Chaosong and Yiyu invited me into Mount Hua and to visit Tianchi, Xuanmu, and Iron Mountain, all famous places. At Cold Mountain the gentlemen Zhao Fanfu, Wen Wenqi, Yao Mengchang, Xu Zhongrong, and Xu Qingzhi asked about the Way at Guanyin Mountain. The two officials Feng Yuancheng and Shen Xuanzhu entertained me at their homes. As I was about to set out, my disciples Dongwen and Hanyue, the grand historian Qian, Wang Jihe, and Qu Wanchu welcomed me to Changshu, and so I came to Mount Yu and lodged two nights. The grand historian of Fushui escorted me to Qu’a, where He Zhiren and his sons and nephews waited at the Sanli Hut at Benniu and asked me to stay in their garden for the summer retreat. I firmly declined and returned to the mountain. The layman He Zhiren gave me the portraits of the eighty-eight patriarchs, painted by the great gentleman Ding Yunpeng, and I accepted them. He escorted me to Jingkou, where I received the vegetarian feast of the black-robed and white-robed of Three Mountains, and in the Dache Hall expounded the precepts for the assembly. When it was done I at once set sail for Mount Kuang, and on the first day of the fifth month passed Baixia, spending a night on the river and seeing one or two old friends. On the fifth I reached Wuhu, where Liu Yushou of the works ministry was supervising the customs barrier and detained me, asking me to write A Discourse on Strange Dreams. The ministry official Cui Helou met me on the river. On the sixteenth day of the fifth month the boat reached Xingzhu, and I arrived at Guizong and lodged there. At that time Minister of War Wang had already provided the funds to build me a quiet hut, and on the fifteenth of the sixth month I ordered my disciple Fushan to begin work at Wuru; by the tenth month one room was finished, and I was able to dwell in peace. Fuzheng observes: in the one age of the Great Ming, the great monks of the Dharma gate who appeared together in the Wanli reign and whose fame overflowed were none other than Lianchi of Yunqi, Daguan Zibo, and Hanshan of Caoxi — the three great elders of the world at that time. He who was the flesh-body heir of the Sixth Patriarch was our Master alone. Our Master, an old veteran of seventy, made one Eastern Journey, and the two stupa inscriptions for Yunqi and Zibo stand as imperishable biographies; the sacrificial texts and likeness-praises fill many leaves with splendour, like the three great elders gathered in conversation. That Fuzheng was able to move among them, staff and sandals, was a rare encounter of his life and a good cause from former lives. In the Eastern Journey Collection that Fuzheng copied out with his own hand, the Essentials of Chan Practice was spoken in the Dharma Hall of Mount Jing, the Essentials of Buddha-Recitation in the Dharma Hall of Yunqi, and the Essentials of Reciting the Cundi in the Zongjing Hall of Jingci. For going west and coming east, and for the various secret gates of mantra-holding, these three instructions leave nothing unstated. Master Da was the first and greatest Dharma friend of our Master’s life; he always regretted that he could not weep face to face for him, and the origin of the Eastern Journey was precisely to settle this first great public case. Master Lian’s accord at Mount Wutai was forty-one years before; Master Yungu’s karmic occasion of sitting in Chan at the Tianjie Temple was fifty-two years before, at the very beginning. These other two great public cases were also settled in the half year of the Eastern Journey. On the day he mourned at Yunqi, more than a thousand black-robed and white-robed pressed him to stay in the mountain. He did not grant their request, but had his portrait painted and left it to be honoured, in expectation of the future, asking that they write a praise themselves. The one who, hearing of Master Lian’s secret practices, wept aloud was Lord Song Huaqing, a disciple of Yunqi. He lingered long at the Zongjing Hall, yet the chronicle omits his surname, for the Dharma occasions of that time were so thronged that its light could not be counted through every crack. And so Fuzheng reflects that in all the chronicle’s course, from Bao’en in Nanking to Jingci by West Lake, the places are so many li apart and the times so many years apart. Of the black-robed and white-robed worthies who took refuge in him in a lifetime, no more than one or two in a thousand are preserved. Yet within its words there is a deep import of its own, which the clear-eyed will be able to fathom for themselves.

That which the chronicle says — that Master Xuanjin and the scholar Tan Mengxun, with the gentry and laymen of the same prefecture, invited him to stay at the Zongjing Hall of Jingci, where for days thousands of fingers were raised around him as he expounded the great precepts, and that he visited Lingyin, the Three Zhu, and the Western Hills and all the famous places — was all a matter of a hundred days. At that time, because the Sacred Mother’s gracious master had been persecuted for spreading the Dharma, and after long garrison duty had returned alive, his fame was truly loud and wide: from the provincial grand coordinators and the regional commanders down to officials great and small of the prefectures and counties, and the faithful of every quarter, officials and laymen, and the elders and younger men of the three gates of Dharma, Vinaya, and Chan, all gathered at Wulin — truly a day worth a thousand years. At that time those who first proposed inviting him from Yunqi and then brought him to Jingci at Nanping were the Renhe magistrate Zhou Jihou, the provincial grand coordinator Jin Xingwu of this region, the ministry official Yu Deyuan, the education commissioner Ge Qizhan, the provincial graduate Wen Qixiang, the official Song Huaqing, the literatus Yan Yinchi, the literatus Zou Mengyang, and other faithful donors. The one who set in order the rules of the cloister and managed the various affairs of providing for the assembly was Master Xuanjin He. At first he put his name to the invitation, and afterwards he followed at his heels to carry out his commands, serving as guest-master and secretary and toiling with the morning lamps: this is indeed a great public case in the whole course of our Master’s Eastern Journey through the three Wu regions. At that time Fuzheng attended him daily, and not a day passed but he trembled as though among dragons, gods, and ghosts. He saw that the Master, as he went about, had never a whisk or a staff; his jade countenance was bright and fair, and in the summer heat he did not sweat; morning and evening when he washed, the water in the vessel was perfectly clear. When he sat he always crossed his legs in full lotus without troubling his hands to arrange them. Closing his eyes he entered samadhi, opening them he left it — by day, by the lamp, walking, standing, sitting, lying. At the least request his eye-light was like lightning, and no speck ever clung to his lids, nor did he trouble his hand to wipe them. After his calamity his feet were slow to walk and he could not stand long; a few paces and he must be supported, a hundred paces and he must be carried. There were four faithful ones who bore him, two from Caoxi and two from Nanyue, who gave up their bodies to serve him over thousands of li and did not leave him for years. From the day in the tenth month of winter of the yiwei year when he received the decree of garrison in Guangdong, the Master let his beard and hair grow, until his long beard was a foot long, and he preached with cap and girdle for twelve years. Down to the eighth month of autumn of the bingwu year, when the imperial eldest grandson had been born and the gracious amnesty released him from the ranks, he had still not been shaved. Nine years more, until he left Guangdong in the jiayin year, and in the fourth month of summer reached Hudong, where he heard that the Sacred Mother had passed into heaven; then he established a bodhimanda of requiting kindness, and in obedience to the gracious edict had his head shaved before the spirit tablet and changed into the monastic dress. Before this he had gone unshaved in Guangdong for fully twenty years. From that shaving to the day in the eleventh month of winter of the bingchen year when he came east to Shuangjing, when Fuzheng first saw the Master’s perfect form, only three years had passed — not long at all. When he ascended the hall to preach, he would open his mouth for thousands of words without swallowing a single one, like a great bell sounding, heard even outside the hall. When he took up the brush to write words of instruction, he did not alter his usual cross-legged posture, and could spread thousands of characters on the paper with no pause in the brush. The attendants who took down his words were worn out running to and fro, with no leisure all day. With his left hand he would turn his bead-string; with his right he would hold a white bamboo folding fan, never out of his hand winter or summer, lifted but not waved, closed but not opened. When some great matter of command arose among men and gods in the three realms, one rap on the desk and none failed to respond. Bamboo clappers and staff, blows and shouts flying — none could match the working of that one fan. It could make demons retire and obey faster than thunder. Of the reaches of his power of the Way and his spiritual penetration that Fuzheng witnessed with his own eyes, he records here a rough account of the greatest. At the Zongjing Hall, one day as he had just ascended the seat, two monks came supporting a third between them up the steps, raving without cease. His two companions begged the Master to rescue him, saying: “This monk has recited the Great Compassion Mantra for five years and has never done a bad deed; we do not know why he has been possessed by a demon to this degree.” The Master said: “This illness can be cured.” At once he ordered an attendant to inquire throughout the hall, and three who had practiced the secret mantra of Ucchuṣma Vajra were found and brought forward. The Master then recited it himself from his seat and had the practitioners pass on the teaching. At first it was not understood; the Master struck the desk with his fan in a display of awe, and as soon as a single phrase was brought up and passed on, the response came like an echo. The practitioners then passed it on phrase by phrase to the end, and the mad monk awakened as from a dream and withdrew after doing reverence. The Master sent him to the incense-kitchen dormitory, and he was as though nothing had been wrong. Those seated there that day included Wu Xingke, the provincial administrator of this province, the Renhe magistrate Zhou Jihou, and the education commissioner Ge

zhan and Yinliang, a whole generation who had never deeply believed, and at this they changed countenance, and the whole assembly was moved. Another day a monk came to do reverence, and before he had risen the Master struck his fan and shouted: “Murderous thief, what do you want with me?” The steward hurried him out. The monk went off without a word, and the assembly stared in astonishment, not understanding. The next day it was heard that he had been arrested for robbery. Such spiritual powers cannot be enumerated. In the two months of his flying staff, every day there was a donor who made an offering of a hundred pieces of gold for the great cauldron of Jingci, boiling ten piculs of rice; whether he stayed or journeyed, not a day passed without lighting the fire. On the day he reached Jiaxing the assembly welcomed him into the Chan hall of the Jinming Temple. The Master ordered Fuzheng to summon his old friends: the minister of war Yue Shifan and the assistant prefect Xiang Chudong, and both came to pay their respects. Chudong, when he held the commission of Kuangzhou, had greatly consorted with the Master and attended him with medicine, settling for a time the judicial officer’s case of demonic possession, and the Master was deeply grateful to him. In their correspondence of that time the Dharma words and handwritten notes were the most numerous. Shifan was wont to make playful talk out of his joy in Chan; formerly, when he was in the ministry of rites and the Master was persecuted for spreading the Dharma, he spoke out boldly to save him. Now they met with great joy. They had scarce sat down and the greetings were not yet done when Yue asked: “Just now I am puzzled by the four phrases on ‘su’ — ‘In wealth and honour, act in wealth and honour; in poverty and meanness, act in poverty and meanness.’ How does the Master explain them?” The Master answered: “Su is a blank sheet of paper: draw a gauze cap and it becomes a gauze cap; draw a beggar and it becomes a beggar.” For in the Ming dynasty officials were called gauze caps. He laughed heartily, and after a while took his leave. At that time, when the feast was done, candles were set out and tea was taken in informal instruction, and the hall door was already shut, when suddenly someone with a staff came shouting outside the door. Some recognized him as the runner Qian of the grain yamen, and took him for a drunken madman; they drove him off but he would not go, and his voice grew shriller, mingled with Buddha-words: “Today the living bodhisattva has come down; I should be delivered. Do not block me.” Fuzheng thought his words strange and told the Master. The Master said: “Call him in.” He came in, joined his palms, and did reverence with the full deportment of a son of the Buddha, and all eyes were upon him. He knelt on both knees and made the bow of a Buddhist. The ghost spoke through him, saying that he was possessed by Qian Da, whose name was Zhong and who was called Ren, and who had borrowed the body to seek deliverance. “Your disciple in life kept a long fast and practiced the Pure Land for eight years. Now the term of my death falls on the fifth seventh-day; I have not gone to the underworld but should be born in the Western Heaven. I beg the bodhisattva in compassion to guide me.” He fell to the ground weeping and wailing without cease. The Master called six elders among the attendants who were devoted to Buddha-recitation to stand by, and himself unrolled the bead-string for him. He at once had a bead-string given to him, and he recited the Buddha’s name a thousand times, and the body the ghost possessed could recite it. The whole hall was solemn and silent. When the recitation was done he had the Mengshan Food-Bestowal Text performed, and when it came to “One should contemplate the nature of the Dharma realm: all is made by mind alone,” he raised his fan, struck the desk, and cried aloud: “Be released at once!” The other answered at once: “Released!” Three calls, three answers, quicker than echo or shadow. He rose again with the full deportment of a Buddhist, gave thanks for rebirth in the Pure Land, bowed east and west to the assembly, and said: “Strive each of you; we shall meet at the Dragon-Flower Assembly.” It was already past the first watch, and the assembly had not dispersed; some wept, some sighed, and some even secretly laughed or murmured, but the Master remained perfectly at ease. As was his custom he must mount his carriage and return to the boat; the other followed the carriage to the cliff’s edge, made reverence and gave thanks, then returned to the gate of the Chan hall and, saying “Thank you, old Master Qian, for the deliverance you obtained by borrowing me,” fell to the ground and woke — and was once more the runner Qian in his usual state. Those nearby said that Ren was a scholar of the Zhong family across the river, the father of Wen Shao, who in life had practiced the Pure Land most devoutly, and that such a response was fitting. Fuzheng replied: “That is my friend of the Bibi Scripture Society, Zhong Shengfu.” At once he went with several of the faithful to knock at the door and drew him over to the Dharma boat to give thanks. Then it was learned that on that day the dead man was exactly in the fifth seventh-day of mourning, and that the runner Qian, coming to press for grain, had entered before his spirit seat and in his drunkenness had drawn the soul to deliverance. In the later examination of the xinyou year Shengfu passed the provincial test. That day there was a relative and friend, the layman Xu Taiwei, long a believer in the Buddha, who, seeing the Master’s spiritual response, invited him to his home, where he had set up the spirit seat of his father, the assistant censor, and begged him to preach the Dharma. Every word the Master spoke revealed the secret affairs of his life, and those who heard were awed into submission. Within a day or two the word spread of the living bodhisattva, and recitation and rumour ran through the city; the elders of the prefecture, children, and women craned their necks as if crazed. Fuzheng attended the Master to Qizhen to do reverence at the stupa of the monk Yungu; then, with carriage and canopy and full deportment, he came to the Eastern Stupa so that the thronging crowd who thirsted for him might have one sight of him and do reverence. In a moment black-robed and white-robed gathered in crowds; from the mountain gate to the abbot’s quarters shoulder pressed heel, and the long causeway and broad platform had no room left to set a foot. So he took counsel with Mr. Yue Shifan to lead the Master in front up the steps to the stupa, and then barred the stupa door. The Master’s frame was great, and they could only support him to the southern railing of the second storey; when the fourfold assembly saw him they bowed in rows and did reverence, rising and falling prostrate to the ground, steaming like cloud and smoke, and only dispersed at nightfall. Lamps were lit as he entered the abbot’s quarters and ascended the seat to preach, giving a few words in brief; then came the feast, and when the feast was done he at once went aboard the boat; those who came bearing incense and offerings of fruit pressed the boat down. The master of the Eastern Stupa hall at that time was Master Jingxiu. The next day the Lengyan invited him to a feast, the master of that hall being Master Maolin. He went through the scripture workshop and inquired into all its rules, and thereupon specially charged Fuzheng with the matter of carving the canon, talking on and on without end. That day the men and women of the city who came to share in the joy also filled the place. The day after that the boat crossed to Songling.

The chronicle also says that the famous worthies of every quarter all gathered about the lake and with the scholar Tan asked about the Dharma, and that the splendour of that southeast Dharma assembly had never been seen before. It also says that of whatever writings he made at the time along the way, Master Xuanjin He and the scholar Tan Mengxun collected four fascicles and printed them under the title Eastern Journey Collection. This was because our Master, at the nirvana assembly, let down his foot as a sign and gave his charge earnestly, singling out the one word “with” — attributing the surpassing cause of the Eastern Journey directly to Fuzheng himself; nowhere in the whole chronicle is there a comparable stroke of approval. In his youth Fuzheng, at the bidding of the late assistant equerry Lord Fantong, was given the courtesy name Mengxun. Afterwards, when his own body lay beneath the collapsed hall and he was saved by the shelter of three beams, it happened that in that very year he met our Master, who gave him the Dharma name Liangsheng. Later he styled himself Sao’an, and people no longer knew him as Mengxun. The verse our Master showed Liangsheng says: “The roof-beam fell and crushed the scholar Tan; being crushed, why did the scholar not die? If the beam had reached the body, the body would be shattered; if the body had reached the beam, the beam would not avoid it. Both have reached — why do they not touch? Ask yourself the reason they do not touch. The illusions before you are not to be compared to a beam; why should the scholar Tan first panic so? If you would not panic, watch a dog driven to leap the wall.” This was the instruction given at their first meeting. Afterwards there were earnest Dharma words given him on holding the Cundi and on the awl-piercing, all recorded in the Eastern Journey Collection. And so he recalls those days: from Shuangjing to Yunqi, invited to stay at the Zongjing Hall of Jingci and to open the hall, then journeying about the lake, Lingyin, Tianzhu, and the various mountains, and to Zhili, Jinming, and the Eastern Stupa, where the light shone greatly; then crossing Songling and Wumen, straight to the Eastern Chan Temple at Jinsha, where he did reverence at his feet and took leave. From spring through summer he attended him with the morning lamps, with no idle day. As the boat was about to be loosed, the Master stroked Fuzheng’s back with his hand and said with a smile: “The affairs after my death I entrust to you.” This was a matter of his twenty-seventh year. Fuzheng’s feeling for the Master was no less than an infant’s craving for the breast; the Master’s care for Fuzheng was no different from a tender mother’s rearing of her child. At that time Fuzheng’s father was at court and his mother in attendance, and the Master, seeing the first signs early, foretold to him the unfinished karmic causes of standing in the world and entering society, and firmly stopped him from following him to Wuru; yet in his gazing and leaning, in dream and sleep, he never forgot him for a moment. From that parting to now his years have reached sixty-two; he is old. All along since receiving the prediction he has held the Cundi, four twelve-year cycles as one day. He sent offerings to Fayun, and the letters that went back and forth fill his boxes. At the Stone Lamp bodhimanda in the capital of Yan he mourned in silence and longing. Only now, face to face with the Dharma image, does he expound the chronicle in commentary, drawing out the instructions of former days and the records he was shown, in hope of settling one day the public case of entering the canon and requesting a posthumous title; and only now does he know that the words of the charge about affairs after death belonged to this very day. Alas, our Master loved Fuzheng as though there were no second in his eyes at the time; and Fuzheng’s service of the Master has perhaps answered to him in some small part.
The Forty-Sixth Year, Wuwu ●

I was seventy-three. The laymen of Wuxia contributed funds to build me the Yilao Hut. That year I began to build the Buddha Hall and the Chan hall at Wuru. In the third month Lord Chen Chishi, assistant administrator of Fuliang, came into the mountain, and with Lord Bao Zhongsu, ministry official of Xin’an, and Lord Xia Woqi, ministry official of Xingzi, formed a society of ten friends to help with the cost of building; by the long-day month the halls were complete. (Chen Chishi, a second time. The ministry official Bao Zhongsu and the ministry official Xia Woqi, once each. Zhongsu was named Ying’ao, a man of Huizhou, and served as chief of the court of imperial sacrifices.)

In the fourth month of summer of the dingyi year, when Fuzheng took leave of our Master, he was charged to collect funds to make an image of the three holy ones of the West coming forth from the mountain — that is, Amitābha, Guanyin, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the lords of the six-period Buddha-recitation bodhimanda, in imitation of Master Yuan’s Lotus Society. This image is rare among the world’s temples, and it happened that a master craftsman of Jiangxi had inherited the art, and the sandalwood carving was exquisite and uncommon. It also happened that a single coiled root of a natural seat was obtained, on which the three holy ones were seated in a row; and again that five ancient bronze censers, vases, candlesticks, and offering vessels were found. In that spring it was completed, and the attendant Master Xuzhong Yi, as the Buddha Hall was about to be finished, came to welcome it, and Fuzheng that same day bought a boat and sent it. At the first sight of it our Master was joyful and praised it, and to this day it is honoured and complete. The halls built at Wuru stand in the prefecture of Jiujiang, county of Dehua, on the shady side of Mount Kuang; at first it was called the Wood-and-Stone Hut, and now it is called the Fayun Temple. The abbot was Master Zhizheng; after his passing it now belongs to Master Ciyan, styled Runhong.
The Forty-Seventh Year, Jiwei ●

I was seventy-four. In the first month of spring I began a long term of reciting the Avatamsaka Sutra and expounded the General Exposition on the Lotus Sutra for the assembly. In summer I expounded the Surangama, the Awakening of Faith, the Diamond, the Perfect Enlightenment, and the Consciousness-Only, the sutras and treatises. In the seventh month of autumn I charged Lord Yuan, prefect of Nankang, to write a record, making Wuru a permanent endowment for the support of the aged of the ten directions. On the fifteenth of the eighth month I shut myself in retreat and cut off all ties, imitating Master Yuan’s practice of burning incense at the six periods in place of the water-clock, and gave my mind wholly to the pure work. I often reflected that the Avatamsaka school was about to lose its transmission: men feared that Qingliang’s subcommentary was too vast, and their minds could not reach it, so most in the world set it aside and relied only on the Combined Treatise. But I thought that Qingliang was the ancestor of composition in this land, and that if he were abandoned the school would lose its lineage. I resolved to take only the subcommentary text and set forth its great purport with the brush, so that readers might easily understand it, entitling it the Essentials; and in the retreat I began to read, revise, and cut it.

Fuzheng observes: in the chronicle the Qingliang public case appears five times, and in the end it is closed with the Essentials of the Avatamsaka. Three years later, in the renxu year, the draft was done — and the karmic occasion of Qingliang was accomplished, and the karmic occasion of Caoxi likewise. Can it be that our Master was Qingliang come again? Moreover, at that very time our Master took the burning of incense in place of the water-clock and made the pure work his whole aim, and yet he could again revise the subcommentary of Qingliang and the whole Avatamsaka school into the Essentials and hand it down to later men: this is what is called the Pure Land as mind-only, the ten thousand dharmas returning to one.
The Forty-Eighth Year, Gengshen — the Accession Year of Taichang ●

I was seventy-five. In spring, outside my lessons, the attendant Guangyi asked me to set forth the Perfect Enlightenment and the Awakening of Faith in direct explanation, and to annotate the seven inner chapters of Zhuangzi. In summer I was ill with a foot ailment. In the eighth month of autumn Lord Chen Wuyi, ministry official of Macheng, Lord Xu Mingheng, ministry official of Anyi, Lord Wu Xunshang, ministry official of Xingzi, Lord Lu Jingye, prefect of Jiangzhou, Lord Yuan Jiuji, prefect of Nankang, and Lord Li Zhongda, the judicial officer, came into the mountain to ask about the Way. The former circuit intendant of Hunan, Lord Wu, now transferred to the Guangdong judgeship, entered Caoxi to do reverence to the Patriarch and asked the disciples in the mountain to send him biographies and praises of the Patriarchs. In my illness I compiled more than seventy short biographies, each with a praise attached, and wrote them out with my own hand. It was already eight years since I had left Caoxi for Nanyue and dwelt at Mount Kuang. The monks of Caoxi longed deeply for my return and sent inquiries again and again, wishing to invite me but unable to. It happened that Lord Wu, going to his post, came into the mountain by the way and saw the work of my restoration, and sighed over it a long while. The monks then told him the whole matter — how they longed for my return and could not obtain it. Lord Wu gladly became their protector of the Dharma and at once sent letters to invite me. The whole assembly of the mountain, with the gentry, elders, and scholars of the province, jointly drew up a petition and came to Mount Kuang to beg me with tears. The Guangdong disciple the censor Wang Xingdong came into the mountain in person three times to invite me, but I firmly declined on account of illness. (Guangyi, a second time. Chen Wuyi, ministry official of Macheng, Xu Mingheng, ministry official of Anyi, Wu Xunshang, ministry official of Xingzi, Lu Jingye, prefect of Jiangzhou, Li Zhongda, judicial officer of Nankang, and Wang Xingdong, censor of Guangdong, once each. Yuan Jiuji, that is Lord Yuan, and Lord Wu, that is Wu Shengbai Zhongwei, a second time each. Jingye was named Menglong, a man of Shanyin in Zhejiang, chief examiner of Guangdong, and served as assistant administrator of Guizhou. Zhongda was named Yingsheng, a man of Jiangyin, an official censor, who was arrested and died in the time of the eunuch Wei.)

Fuzheng observes: in the chronicle the first entry is that in the eighth month of autumn of the tenth year of Wanli, the renwu year, the crown prince was born; the second entry, that in the eighth month of autumn of the thirty-fourth year the imperial eldest grandson was born; the third entry, the forty-eighth year, gengshen, which is the change of reign-title to Taichang. For on the twenty-sixth day of the seventh month of that year the Shenzong Emperor died and Taichang ascended, and an edict decreed that the next year should be the first year of Taichang. On the third day of the ninth month of that year the Guangzong Emperor in turn died, and on the sixth day Tianqi ascended. The supervising official Li Ruogui and the investigating censor Zuo Guangdou petitioned that from the first day of the eighth month to the end of the twelfth month the reign-title Wanli be dropped and the days be styled the first year of Taichang, borrowed from the late emperor; in the end it was not approved. This too failed in the meaning of a proper beginning and a proper ending, and came of a moment’s groundless expedient, closing the matter in haste. To borrow from the late emperor and so diminish the calendar years, which is unfilial toward the one who died later, is worse than to borrow from the later emperor and so make plain the first year of sacrifice, which is filial toward the newly ascended. Moreover, to take the first year of Tianqi as the first year of Taichang is precisely to believe that the edict of Taichang’s accession was no borrowing. The second year of Tianqi was in truth the first year of Tianqi. Now the first year of Taichang can only be appended in a side-note under the forty-eighth year of Wanli. Our Master feared that this change of reign-title would be buried, and therefore writes it large and twice under the forty-eighth year, gengshen: “the change of reign-title to Taichang.” These five characters are the greatest instance of the brush-method and heart-method of the Spring and Autumn; how could they have been met with in the chronicles of former Patriarchs? The prayer for an heir at Mount Wutai, the protection of the heir at the Cishou Temple, and even the interrogation at the Zhenfu Office and the garrison service beyond the Dayu Ridge — what Chancellor Zhang Hongyang called his great hidden service to the altars of state — all come to one great conclusion in these five characters. In the intervals of the incense-clock and Buddha-recitation at Wuru, to expound, annotate, and compose, preaching ardently without an empty day — how could that be within the power of an old man of seventy-five, and ill at that? The work of Wuru was unfinished and the work of Caoxi revived: this is what is called “Heaven’s movement is strong; the gentleman strengthens himself without cease.” My friend Wang Jiyan, whose name was Qilong, wrote A Debate on the First Year of Taichang and Doubts Raised, examining back and forth in detail the regulations of reign-changes in ancient and modern times, some two thousand characters with all his strength, and truly he first spoke my own mind. His main point is that a change of reign-title after the year has passed is the constant rule for all ages, and that changing it with the month is the error of a moment — two phrases cover it. He also says that if a year can be divided into two sections, then since Wanli, Taichang, and Tianqi all fall within one year, why can it not be divided into three? That is a forced and disjointed argument, making the Guangzong temple a mere wart. These words open the eyes and pierce the heart still more; my poor view had not reached so far. Moreover, the Guangzong Emperor’s sagely virtue was lofty and generous, and he was a lord not to be produced in a generation: in the month of his accession the Yellow River at Lingong in Shaanxi ran clear for three days. He early stopped the mining taxes by decree, recalled all the tax eunuchs, and sent out treasury gold to reward the frontier to the amount of a million; he summoned back the outspoken officials who had offered advice, as though he had no leisure even to eat — and this is only what the new government accomplished. As for his nurturing of virtue in the Eastern Palace, his benevolence and filial piety were exhaustively devoted, when within there were the forms of flourishing and withering and without the provocations of partisans; to stand in such a place was truly hard. When the Shenzong Emperor was about to die he decreed that the Honoured Consort Zheng be made empress and charged him to carry it out; the court officials disputed it, yet in the end he could not bear to take it from her. These forty days of filial thought and benevolent grace reached to three reigns — the way of Heaven may still be asked about. So, because in the Patriarch Hanshan’s chronicle there stand the five characters “the change of reign-title to Taichang,” Fuzheng was moved and noted it.
In that year there was a letter showing Fuzheng his intention of going to Caoxi, and he wrote beforehand an inscription for the layman Tan, provincial graduate.
The First Year of Tianqi, Xinyou ●

I was seventy-six. In summer, at the request of the assembly, I expounded the Surangama Notes. In the tenth month of winter my disciples, the provincial graduates Liu Qixiang, Chen Dixiang, Chen Dichun, and Liang Sixiang, came to inquire after me. At that time the former observer of Shaoyang, Lord Zhu, now transferred to the Guangdong sea circuit, together with Lord Wu, sent letters and came again to Mount Kuang, and I again declined on account of illness. (Liu Qixiang, Chen Dixiang, Chen Dichun, and Liang Sixiang, once each. Lord Zhu, the former Xingcun, a second time; Lord Wu, the former Shengbai, a third time.)

Lord Zhu Xingcun and Lord Wu Shengbai, two elders of Fuzheng’s own district and both men of Yanguan, were in the end able to bring about the gathering of the flesh-bodies of the Sixth Patriarch and the Patriarch Hanshan — so great a karmic occasion. In this year, though he had not yet returned to Caoxi, the first signs of return had already stirred and the momentum of return was decided. Had he not returned to Caoxi again, then even though his flesh-body came forth from Wuru, without coming face to face with Patriarch Lu there would have been no great marvel.
The above closes the public case of the Fayun Temple at Wuru on Mount Kuang.
The Second Year, Renxu ●

I was seventy-seven. I pressed on with the Essentials of the Avatamsaka, and the draft was done. The assembly asked me to expound the Surangama, the Perfect Enlightenment, the Diamond, the Awakening of Faith, and the Zhao Lun, and the various sutras and treatises. When Lord Wu returned from his audience at court he sent letters again, his meaning the more urgent; and Lord Zhang Sanxing, prefect of Shaoyang, sent a special letter and dispatched the hall master Ben’ang to me. My feelings left me no choice, and I resolved that I must go. On the tenth day of the eleventh month, at the winter solstice of that year, I left Mount Kuang and crossed Lake Peng, and wrote poems. Before long Lord Zou Nangao, the chief of the academy, returning north, sought me in the mountain. By then I had reached Jizhou, and met the grand historian Xiao Zhuoxiu, Ma Jifang, Zeng Yaochen, Liu Shaoye, He Keshang, and Liu Zhuanhua, who asked about the Way at the Ziyan Mountain House. On the eighth day of the twelfth month I crossed the ridge, and on the fifteenth entered Caoxi. (Lord Wu Shengbai, a fourth time. Lord Zhang Sanxing, prefect of Shaoyang, and the hall master Ben’ang, once each. Lord Zou Nangao, chief of the academy, a second time. The grand historian Xiao Zhuoxiu, Ma Jifang, Zeng Yaochen, Liu Shaoye, He Keshang, and Liu Zhuanhua, once each. Sanxing was named Yizhen, a man of Huating in Songjiang, who rose from prefect of Shaozhou to assistant commissioner of Guangxi. Zhuoxiu was named Yunju, styled Xuanpu, registered in Xuanhua of Guangxi, a man of Taihe in Jiangxi, and served as junior minister.)

Fuzheng observes: Lord Nangao and those after him were all men of Jiangxi of firm principle and of the Dharma, noted in the last leaves; they were chosen out of many and only a few taken, and in the end he never gave his approval to any one of them. Confucius at seventy-two, in the tenth month of winter, composed the Spring and Autumn, laying down his brush at the capture of the qilin in the western hunt; the next year, at seventy-three, he dreamed of the offerings and sang his last song. The Patriarch Hanshan at seventy-seven, on the fifteenth of the twelfth month, composed the chronicle, laying down his brush at the crossing of the ridge and his entry into Caoxi; the next year, at seventy-eight, his flesh-body passed into cessation. The sage before and the sage after fit like the two halves of a tally — how should one speak of Confucian and Buddhist appearances? Still more marvellous: our Master, during his former stay in Guangdong, twenty-one years from first to last, was never shaved. Only when he came to Chu did he assume the perfect form and return to the monastic dress. Had he not returned again to Caoxi, then the black-robed and white-robed of Guangdong would never in their lives have seen our Master’s perfect form in monastic dress. Yet whether with hair or without, in monastic or Confucian dress, wherein the sages differ and agree does not lie here at all.

Fuzheng was able to see the works of our Master: the Surangama Notes, the Essentials of the Avatamsaka, the Beating the Beat on the Lotus, the Hanging Mirror on the Surangama, the General Exposition on the Surangama, the General Exposition on the Lotus, the Explanation of the Awakening of Faith, the Explanation of the Consciousness-Only Treatise, the Direct Explanation of the Perfect Enlightenment, the Treatise on the Influence of Laozi and Zhuangzi, the Explanation of the Classic of the Dao and its Virtue, the Explanation of the Seven Inner Chapters of Zhuangzi, the Hanshan Preface, the Direct Pointing at the Doctrine of the Mean, the Doubts Resolved on the Great Learning, the Heart-Method of the Zuo Commentary to the Spring and Autumn Annals, the Palm-Guide to the Qimen, the Dream-Wandering Collection, and the Gazetteer of Caoxi. Those that Fuzheng copied out with his own hand and sent to the block were the Eastern Journey Collection; and printed, the Doubts Resolved on the Diamond. His writings are many more. As he said face to face, there are the Treatise on the Three Teachings, the General Explanation of the Analects, and the Palm-Guide to the Qimen. And as Jianru said, there are the Complete Recorded Sayings in a certain number of fascicles, which after our Master’s passing were stolen and sold elsewhere by the attendant Xinqi and cannot now be seen; these are not recorded in full. What the wisdom-life of the Buddha and the Patriarchs rests upon is the Surangama Notes first and the Essentials of the Avatamsaka last. The school does not depart from the teaching, the Patriarch does not depart from the Buddha: in these it is most manifest and notable. Our Master often said of himself that whatever came from his brush or tongue was always gathered in spirit and entered into contemplation, realizing accord with the Buddha’s mind; if it smacked ever so little of thought and deliberation, it was of no use. And this Essentials of the Avatamsaka, whose draft was completed, belongs to the year before his passing into cessation at seventy-seven, standing in place of Sakyamuni’s last holding up of the flower between the twin trees. His power of samadhi and his spiritual light, vigorous and unceasing, are fully present in the palm-leaf books of the Mahāyāna: how could thought and deliberation reach so far?
In that year began the karmic occasion of his return to Caoxi, leaving unfinished the public case of a Hanshan temple and the flesh-body succession to the Patriarch.
Here ends the Commentary on the Veritable Record of the Old Man of Hanshan’s Own Chronicle.
Appendix
Thirty-Six Praises of the Ancient Buddha in the Flesh Who Restored Caoxi, the Patriarch-Successor Hanshan (with Preface and Titles)

I sigh in secret that the maṇi jewel is priceless, and that one seldom meets a merchant who can tell it. The poor son loses his treasure only because he has long been lost on the road home. That is why students of the Way are as many as the hairs of a cow, while those who awaken the mind are as rare as the horns of a qilin. I was born out of season, to meet the autumn of change and vicissitude; how fortunate am I in body to see the day when the ancient Buddha appears. This udumbara flower of Caoxi bloomed once three thousand years ago; the cause and fruit of the flesh-body meet again after five hundred lives. Dwelling where he should not dwell, he dwells in this body, and the ten thousand things are complete in me. Attaining where there is nothing to attain, he attains his place; and turning back upon himself and becoming sincere, there is no greater joy. Great Master Yongjia has said: “The three bodies and four wisdoms are perfected within the essence; the eight liberations and six penetrations are the seal of the mind-ground.” Now the flesh-body bodhisattva, Great Master Hanshan, with just this mind-seal, seals all once and for all, and there is no other dharma. One gate steps beyond samādhi and dhyāna, one gate enters straight into the wondrous adorned path. No need of clay or wood, of red or blue pigment: the Dharma-body fills the void. Why need of golden terraces and silver pavilions, when his image shines through the Dharma realm? Yet ignorant worldlings still complain that he went about in cangue and chains, driving his stake and pulling his oar. So, reading his chronicle, I set out its titles and made these thirty-six praises, in compliance with the request of Tan, the director of education, of Sao’an.
(A White-Robed Rebirth) ●

Not in the middle, nor within, nor yet without — he leaves the world more thirsting and more devout. The soiled robe, how could he bear to cast it down? I fear that beings will scarcely grasp it, one and all.
(The Knot of Doubt over Birth and Death) ●

Ere he had found the road to serve the King of Emptiness, he already knew to drill for light within the smoke. He burned up the three thousand great thousand worlds, and sought life within death — a marvellous device.
(Requiting Kindness and Attaining Deliverance) ●

Old Lu, who handed on the robe, was then no monk; he smiled at old Cai who trudged the dusty road. To give this body and mind to lands as countless as dust — this, and this alone, is requiting the Buddha’s grace.
(The Vow to Restore) ●
Leaving home, he meant to save all living beings; why then bring disaster on a whole temple of monks? He saved a crowd of men who had nothing to do, and the adorned precious hall is in his own body.
(Going to the Capital to Seek Instruction) ●
Wrongly setting down those words of Yongjia: to seek a master and ask the Way is to investigate Chan. Had he not entered the wave that startles men, how could fish and dragons leap into his boat?
(Meeting the Master in Willow Lane) ●

The black dragon’s pearl he picked up, a jewel for the house; would he let it fall into another’s ten-thousand-fathom pit? Though this land of Zhen is broad, there is no other road; for a while he borrows the feet of sons and grandsons to walk it.
(Meeting a Friend at the Capital Gate) ●
Through you the mind-seal knows its former face; like answers like, with no fine shavings left. The frontier goose was not startled up by men; the wind struck the reed-mist and filled the blue sky.
(Lying in the Snow at Mount Tai) ●

He would test the lotus within the red-hot furnace; fine gold, a hundred times refined, shines the brighter. A ball of snow in his hand, he strikes where it is easy — and only then feels the coolness surpass all talk of Chan.
(Hiding Together in the Western Hills) ●

The Tathagatas of the three ages speak with a single voice; only then one knows how many kalpas he lay as if asleep. In me there is nothing hidden from you; every bit is so — the osmanthus fragrance fills all, and one wonders at so many words.
(Capital for Dwelling in the Mountain) ●

A poor man in the mountain, without a single string of cash; he calls on Heaven again and again in bitter cry. The eighty thousand Dharma gates enter from here — much like a trader who has got his capital at last.
(Reverencing the Patriarch at Shaolin) ●
The blue-eyed barbarian monk came into Han; nine years — why was his mouth so hard to open? Today he has caught and beaten that stinking bearded one, and shapes a fist to smite him in the face.
(Not Meeting Daqian) ●
They said there was a Daqian at Mount Song, and to this day the Shaolin Chan is unbroken. Had he known earlier not to go to Mount Song, he would have spared the beings who lick at wild spittle.
(Joyfully Meeting Faguang) ●
Faguang took up his staff and chased the rabbit; then turned and flung it back to strike the toad. The dead snake he did not cut but let it go, and boasts before men of the Chan school’s play.
(Listening to the Water at Dragon Gate) ●

He did not walk where the people of the time walked, but came to the bridge side to listen to the stream. Suddenly he stamped and cut the road of the stream’s sound: the ear hears nothing, and the eye is blind too.
(Rising from Samadhi, Dust on the Cauldron) ●

How many times the flowers bloomed and their shadows climbed the wall; on the crystal hall there is no news at all. The axe-handle rotted, and he did not know the years; the gibbons cried all night — did they ever cease?
(Protecting Mount Tai) ●
Who can measure the breadth of Mount Tai? Year after year the emperor’s million bushels of grain. How could this matter be explained? One look from Lord Hu, and there was no harm.
(Intercourse with the Holy Assembly) ●
If you do not know the man, look at his friends: Mañjuśrī and Maitreya expose the family’s shame. Dreaming awakening, awakening dreaming — all alike; were I to see it, I would hurry to beat the dog.
(The Birth of an Imperial Heir) ●

Pointing to heaven and earth when the Buddha was first born; the five positions of lord and minister — he is the honoured one. The imperial prince of the Great Ming is like the Buddha: the maṇi pearl appears and sets heaven and earth at rest.
